newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh budget aims to boost growth,help poor.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh budget aims to boost growth,help poor.

text.p: Bangladesh on Thursday unveiled a deficit budget for fiscal 1997/98 which the government said would improve the lives of millions of poor people and spur the country's development.

The budget placed before parliament by Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria proposed a 81.62 billion taka ($1.9 billion) deficit for fiscal 1997/98, running from July to June. Revenue was envisaged at 196.24 billion taka against expenditure of 277.86 billion.

Kibria also forecast more robust growth over the next few years, predicting annual Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would expand by 7.0 percent between fiscal 1997/98 and 2001/2, against an average 4.5 percent during 1991-96.
The country's economy grew by 5.7 percent in 1996/97 against a target of 5.5 percent. GDP growth was 5.4 percent in 1995/96.
"The economic policies pursued by the government paved the way for this success," Kibria said.
The finance minister proposed higher taxes for private cars and electronic goods, while lowering them for imports of public transports like bus and trucks.

In a bid to boost business activity, Kibria proposed to cut corporate tax for banks, insurance companies and financial institutions to 40 percent from 45 percent. He also proposed reducing the highest rate of customs duty to 42.5 percent for 1997/98 from the present 45 percent.

"We will incur substantial revenue loss due to this reduction -- but such tariff reduction is essential...in keeping with the global trend of trade liberalisatiuon and to promote efficiency in the economy," he said.
The measures immediately came under attack from the main opposition Bangladesh Natiaonalist Party (BNP).

"The budget is not encouraging and faulty. It has not reflected the realities," said BNP central leader and former finance minister Saifur Rahman. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's government had failed to manage the economy since it took office one year ago, and there had been capital flight rather than increases in investment, he said.
According to the budget summary statement, the deficit would be compensated for by expected foreign assistance worth 53.42 billion taka, as well as money raised from borrowing on domestic markets.
But Kibria said the country's revenue to GDP (gross domestic product) ratio was only 12 percent compared with 20, 19, and 18 percent in Sri Lanka, India and Pakistan respectively.
"This weakness in our revenue mobilisation effort has not only resulted in a shortage of funds to finance our development needs but has also become an impediment to rapid economic growth," he said.
The budget allocated 23.3 percent of its spending to alleviate poverty, with subsidies for agriculture, housing and a monthly pension allowance for 450,000 poverty-stricken elderly people.
This included setting up a 0.5 billion taka pension fund, a 0.5 billion taka housing fund and providing credit worth up to 10 billion taka for the country's cereal-growers.
"This is an insufficient measure in the backdrop of pervasive poverty. But it's an experiment and only a beginning," Kibria said.
Dr. Atiur Rahman, senior research fellow of Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies, described the budget as conservative and pragmatic.

"The finance minister tried to keep the balance (in the budget) despite pressure from declining foreign exchange reserves and low investment in industry," he said. But he warned that the measures set out were not enough to fight poverty and generate employment.
